title: The US Just Fined an Indian-Origin Attorney $255,000 for Filing Fake Asylum Claims. It Has Never Done That Before.
excerpt: DHS says California-based Vinod Doddamani submitted 64 nearly identical asylum declarations on behalf of Indian nationals — and the penalty signals a much broader crackdown.
body:
The Department of Homeland Security has fined an Indian-origin immigration attorney more than $255,000 for allegedly filing dozens of fraudulent asylum claims on behalf of Indian nationals — the first time the agency has ever sought financial penalties against a lawyer for this kind of misconduct.

Vinod Doddamani, a California-based attorney who operates a nationwide practice representing mostly Indian immigrants, was hit with five Notices of Intent to Fine by Homeland Security Investigations on June 22. The agency alleges that across 32 immigration cases, Doddamani submitted 64 fraudulent documents — asylum declarations that were, in DHS's words, "identical or nearly identical in language and substance, containing the same or nearly the same factual narrative and supporting details regarding the alleged persecution."

In plain terms: the same story of persecution, recycled across dozens of different clients.

## A First-of-Its-Kind Enforcement Action

What makes this case extraordinary is not just its scale, but the mechanism. Before this month, DHS had never attempted to fine an attorney for filing false asylum claims. The legal authority to do so came from a directive issued in May by DHS General Counsel James Percival, who instructed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to begin pursuing attorneys suspected of submitting fraudulent applications in immigration courts.

"The days of attorneys abusing and defrauding our immigration system are OVER," DHS posted on X, announcing the action. "Our message to immigration attorneys is clear: if you engage in fraud, you will be held ACCOUNTABLE."

Percival framed the crackdown in national security terms: "Fraudulent asylum claims threaten the safety of Americans by overwhelming our burdened immigration system and delaying the removal of dangerous criminal aliens."

The fine — $255,232 in total — has not yet been finalized through adjudication. Doddamani has not publicly commented on the allegations.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

The case lands at a particularly fraught moment for Indian immigrants in the United States. The Trump administration has spent the past year tightening every legal immigration pathway — canceling student visas, imposing a now-struck-down $100,000 H-1B fee, expanding travel bans, and deploying ICE enforcement operations at an unprecedented pace.

For the Indian community specifically, the optics are damaging. Indians represent one of the largest groups of asylum seekers processed through US immigration courts, and any high-profile fraud case involving Indian nationals risks fueling a narrative that the administration has been building: that the system is being systematically exploited.

Immigration attorneys who work with Indian clients say the real danger is a chilling effect. Legitimate asylum seekers — people fleeing genuine religious, caste-based, or political persecution — may now face higher scrutiny and greater skepticism from immigration judges who have seen a steady drumbeat of fraud headlines.

"The problem is not that DHS is going after bad actors — it should," said one immigration lawyer who represents Indian clients in New York, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The problem is when every Indian asylum case gets painted with the same brush."

## A Pattern of Escalation

The Doddamani case is part of a broader enforcement wave that has specifically named Indian nationals in recent months. In March, the FBI charged eleven Indian nationals in Massachusetts with conspiracy to commit visa fraud through staged robberies designed to support U Visa applications. In a separate case, ten more Indian nationals were indicted on similar charges in Boston.

Meanwhile, ICE recently disclosed what it called an "uncontrolled" fraud scheme involving thousands of foreign students and "phantom employees" — a case that also disproportionately involved Indian nationals enrolled at pay-to-stay institutions.

The pattern is unmistakable: Indian immigrants are showing up in a disproportionate number of high-profile immigration fraud cases, creating a political liability for a community that has historically been associated with legal, skilled migration.

## What Happens Next

The DHS enforcement action against Doddamani is civil, not criminal — he faces a fine, not prosecution. But legal experts say the case is likely a test run. If the penalty sticks, it will establish a precedent that makes it far easier for DHS to go after other attorneys, and potentially seek larger fines.

The First Circuit Court of Appeals is already reviewing several immigration-related rulings, including the court order that struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee. The legal architecture around immigration enforcement is in flux, and the Doddamani case adds another brick.

For the roughly 4.8 million Indian-origin residents in the United States, the message is hard to miss: the era of lax enforcement is over, and the scrutiny extends not just to immigrants themselves, but to the professionals who represent them.

*Sources: Department of Homeland Security, Fox News, News Dive, Newspoint, Wealth of Geeks*
